newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Ministers reject wider action to protect against BSE.
newsitem.headline: Ministers reject wider action to protect against BSE.

text.p: European Union farm ministers on Tuesday rejected a proposal to ban from the human food chain offal from sheep and goats that can harbour scrapie or mad cow disease.
The European Commission said the measure was needed after British and French research showed that sheep could catch mad cow disease -- Bovine Spongiform Encephalopathy (BSE).
Suspect offal from cattle is already banned.
"It's a regrettable decision," EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler told a news conference after a two-day meeting.
Only France, Britain, Ireland, Sweden and Luxembourg voted in favour of EU-wide measures while 10 countries voted against.
Under special EU voting rules, a simple majority of eight member states was required to throw out the proposal.
"Prions don't know the Schengen agreement," Fischler earlier told ministers, referring to the infective BSE agent and a pact under which seven EU member states ended border controls.
Fischler said he will make fresh proposals in a few months time after EU veterinary inspectors have issued reports.
French Agriculture Minister Philippe Vasseur agreed that the proposal was a necessary safety measure.
"We don't take out an insurance policy to have an accident but as a precaution," he told reporters.

But most member states were unconvinced, saying the measure was unnecessary and economically excessive given that their countries were virtually free of BSE and scrapie, a similar brain-wasting disease that has affected sheep for centuries.
Germany, supported by others, argued that the measure should be targeted on countries worst hit by the diseases.
Earlier this month, only Britain and France had supported the proposal when it was put to a vote by the EU's Standing Veterinary Committee of senior national officials.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler refused to make concessions, arguing that no country was totally risk-free and national exemptions would distort trade in the 15-nation bloc.

The Commission's proposal, based on advice from EU vets and the World Health Organistion, involved the removal of brains, eyes, spinal cord and spleen from sheep, cattle and goats over 12 months old to keep it out of human and animal food.
